difficultyReason: Two-premise medical argument. The gap is a hidden equivalence between the experimental marker (inflammation) and the clinical outcome (arthritis), and a reference-class trap is available. Negating the correct answer severs the marker-to-disease bridge.
stimulus: Researcher: Patients who took the experimental compound Relvanix for six months showed significantly lower levels of joint inflammation than a comparable group who took a placebo. Since elevated joint inflammation is a precursor to osteoarthritis in older adults, we conclude that Relvanix will reduce the incidence of osteoarthritis among older adults who take it.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Relvanix produces no side effects more serious than the osteoarthritis it is intended to prevent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing joint inflammation through means other than Relvanix would also lower the incidence of osteoarthritis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reduction in joint inflammation produced by Relvanix is sufficient to decrease the rate at which osteoarthritis develops.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most older adults who develop osteoarthritis have previously exhibited elevated joint inflammation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No medication currently on the market reduces joint inflammation as effectively as Relvanix does.

explanations.correct: The argument leaps from 'Relvanix lowers inflammation' to 'Relvanix prevents osteoarthritis.' Inflammation being a precursor does not guarantee that any reduction in it is large enough to change disease rates. Negate C — the reduction is not sufficient — and the conclusion about osteoarthritis incidence falls apart.
explanations.A: Out of scope — side effects are not a link in the inflammation-to-arthritis inference.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — the argument concerns Relvanix specifically, not alternative means of reducing inflammation.
explanations.D: Reversed direction — the argument needs inflammation reduction to prevent arthritis, not that arthritis patients had inflammation.
explanations.E: Too strong and off-point — relative efficacy against other drugs is not required for the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Economic argument relies on a conditional about consumer behavior. The necessary assumption rules out a specific alternative explanation (stockpiling) that would otherwise undermine the causal claim.
stimulus: Economist: In the month after the city imposed a new tax on sugary drinks, sales of those drinks within city limits dropped by nearly 30 percent. Clearly, the tax has succeeded in discouraging residents from consuming sugary drinks.
questionStem: The economist's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: residents did not stockpile significant quantities of sugary drinks before the tax took effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: the tax revenue collected will be used to fund public health programs

choices.label: C
choices.text: sugary drinks are the leading cause of preventable illness in the city

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other city has imposed a comparable tax on sugary drinks

choices.label: E
choices.text: the tax applies equally to all sugary drinks sold in the city

explanations.correct: The argument infers reduced consumption from reduced post-tax sales. If residents had stockpiled before the tax took effect, post-tax sales would drop even though total consumption was unchanged. Negate A and the sales drop no longer shows discouraged consumption.
explanations.B: Out of scope — how revenue is used has no bearing on whether the tax discouraged consumption.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the conclusion is about this tax's effect, not about the overall health importance of sugary drinks.
explanations.D: Irrelevant comparison — other cities' taxes are not a link in the inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — uniform application is not required for the sales drop to reflect reduced consumption.

difficultyReason: Historical argument with a chronological subtlety: the coin's presence at the site only dates the settlement if the coin arrived during occupation rather than later. Several close-cousin distractors.
stimulus: Archaeologist: A silver coin minted between 180 and 160 B.C.E. was unearthed last summer in a soil layer at the Helvetian hill settlement. This strongly suggests that the settlement was inhabited during the second century B.C.E.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the archaeologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coins from this mint circulated widely throughout the region during the second century B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other artifacts at the settlement have been dated to earlier than the second century B.C.E.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coin was not deposited in that soil layer long after the settlement was abandoned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most inhabitants of the settlement would have handled silver coins at some point in their lives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The coin was minted within a few years of reaching the settlement.

explanations.correct: The argument dates occupation from the coin's presence. If the coin was dropped at the site centuries after the settlement was abandoned (by a later traveler, a burial, soil disturbance), the coin tells us nothing about when the site was inhabited. Negate C and the inference collapses.
explanations.A: Too strong — wide circulation is not required for a single coin to reach the site during occupation.
explanations.B: Out of scope — other artifacts' dates are not a link in this particular inference.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — whether most inhabitants handled coins is irrelevant to dating the settlement from this coin.
explanations.E: Too strong — the coin could have reached the site decades after minting and still fall within the occupation period.

difficultyReason: Environmental argument pivots on a reference-class assumption: the studied wetlands must be representative of the ones the policy would protect. Strong distractors invoke related scope.
stimulus: Environmental analyst: Wetlands in the Bayou Tertre region that have been fenced off from cattle over the past decade have regenerated native grasses at three times the rate of unfenced wetlands. Therefore, a statewide policy that fences cattle out of wetlands would significantly accelerate native-grass regeneration across the state.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wetlands outside the Bayou Tertre region do not differ from those within it in ways that would prevent fencing from having the same effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cattle are the most significant threat to native grasses in the state's wetlands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No native grasses will regenerate in wetlands that remain accessible to cattle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost of fencing cattle out of wetlands statewide will not exceed the ecological benefits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ranchers in the Bayou Tertre region were legally required to fence their cattle out of wetlands.

explanations.correct: The argument generalizes from Bayou Tertre to the whole state. If wetlands elsewhere differ in ways that defeat the fencing effect (different grass species, different soil, other dominant pressures), the generalization fails. Negate A and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument needs only that fencing helps, not that cattle are the single leading threat.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion requires acceleration, not that unfenced wetlands regenerate nothing.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — cost-benefit is not part of the regeneration-rate inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — what motivated the Bayou Tertre fencing is not a link in the argument.

difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning argument with a hidden conditional: the conclusion that the ordinance is void requires not only a conflict but that state law prevail over municipal law in this area. The defender-style assumption is easy to overlook.
stimulus: Legal analyst: The city's new ordinance forbids short-term rentals of residential property for fewer than thirty days. But state law grants property owners the right to rent their homes for any length of time they choose. Consequently, the city's ordinance is unenforceable.
questionStem: The analyst's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most homeowners in the city would prefer to rent their property for fewer than thirty days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The state legislature has the exclusive authority to regulate all real-estate transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a municipal ordinance conflicts with state law on this subject, state law prevails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city had no legitimate reason to restrict short-term rentals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have previously struck down similar short-term rental ordinances in other cities.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes the conflict between the ordinance and state law resolves in favor of state law — otherwise the ordinance remains enforceable despite the conflict. Negate C and the conclusion no longer follows.
explanations.A: Out of scope — homeowner preferences are not a link in the enforceability inference.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument needs state law to prevail on this subject, not exclusive state authority over all real-estate matters.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — whether the city's reasons are legitimate is irrelevant to legal enforceability against state law.
explanations.E: Out of scope — what other courts have done is not cited as a premise in this argument.

difficultyReason: Technology argument relies on a hidden bridge between a security metric (password strength) and the conclusion (reduced breaches). The assumption must rule out the main alternative cause of breaches.
stimulus: Technology consultant: Last year our firm rolled out a password manager that generated long, randomized passwords for every employee account. Since then, the number of successful breaches of employee accounts has dropped by more than half. The password manager has clearly been the key to improving our security.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the consultant's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee at the firm uses the password manager for each of their accounts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other change made during the past year was largely responsible for the drop in successful breaches.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Randomized passwords are harder to crack than any passwords employees would have chosen themselves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Successful breaches of employee accounts had been increasing before the password manager was introduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The password manager's randomized passwords cannot be recovered even by the manager's developer.

explanations.correct: The argument credits the password manager for the drop in breaches. If some other change (new firewall, staff training, phishing filter) was largely responsible, the causal claim fails. Negate B and the conclusion loses its support.
explanations.A: Too strong — the argument needs the manager to drive the drop, not universal adoption.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion needs the manager to have contributed to the drop, not that its passwords are uncrackable-relative-to-every-alternative.
explanations.D: Out of scope — a pre-existing trend is not required by the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope — developer access is not a link in the causal claim.

difficultyReason: Linguistic argument hinges on a subtle equivalence between a writing system's age and the language's age. Several distractors mimic the correct answer's scope.
stimulus: Linguist: Inscriptions written in the Turvanic script have been recovered from sites dated to at least 3,200 years ago. Because the Turvanic script was used exclusively to record the Turvanic language, we conclude that the Turvanic language was spoken at least 3,200 years ago.
questionStem: The linguist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Turvanic script was not developed significantly earlier than it began to be used for inscriptions

choices.label: B
choices.text: the inscriptions were produced by people who were native speakers of the Turvanic language

choices.label: C
choices.text: any language used for inscriptions at a site must have been spoken at that site

choices.label: D
choices.text: the Turvanic script was the only script in use in the region 3,200 years ago

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Turvanic language was not used exclusively for ceremonial purposes at the time of the inscriptions

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the language was spoken, based on an inscribed script. But a script can be used to record a language that was not actually spoken by the inscribers (a liturgical or imported language, as with Latin in medieval Europe). The bridge needed is that the script was being used to record a spoken language at the time. Negate B — the inscribers did not speak Turvanic — and the conclusion that Turvanic was spoken 3,200 years ago loses support.
explanations.A: Shift in subject — the conclusion is about the language, not about when the script was invented.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument needs only that someone spoke Turvanic, not that every inscribed language was locally spoken.
explanations.D: Out of scope — other scripts' presence doesn't affect the Turvanic inference.
explanations.E: Reversed direction — this rules out ceremonial-only use, which is close, but the argument actually needs the stronger claim that speakers produced the inscriptions; E alone permits a script without any living speakers using it.

difficultyReason: Arts/aesthetics argument contains a category-bridge: a 'mastery of perspective' attribution requires ruling out that the work is a later copy. Sharp negation test.
stimulus: Art historian: The recently discovered panel depicting a market square uses precise single-point perspective of a kind not developed until the 1420s. The panel is signed by Pietro di Marco, who died in 1398. Since works signed by Pietro are almost never forged, we may conclude that Pietro anticipated single-point perspective by more than two decades.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The panel was not painted by a later artist and signed with Pietro's name for commercial reasons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pietro di Marco was the most accomplished painter of his generation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other painter working before 1420 made use of single-point perspective.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The perspective techniques developed in the 1420s were based on Pietro's work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The market square depicted on the panel was a familiar subject for painters of Pietro's era.

explanations.correct: The argument infers Pietro's authorship from the signature, then credits Pietro with anticipating perspective. If a later artist painted the panel and appended Pietro's signature (even without a forgery's typical intent to deceive collectors), Pietro didn't anticipate anything. Negate A and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.B: Out of scope — Pietro's overall standing isn't a link in the inference.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion is about Pietro's anticipation, not a universal claim about all pre-1420 painters.
explanations.D: Reversed direction — the argument doesn't claim the 1420s techniques derived from Pietro.
explanations.E: Out of scope — subject matter is not part of the reasoning.

difficultyReason: Policy argument moves from a program's prior effectiveness to a prediction about the current case. The necessary assumption guards against a relevant change in conditions.
stimulus: Policy adviser: The tutoring program that we implemented in Millbrook's public schools five years ago improved student reading scores by an average of 12 percent within two years. Our neighboring district has demographics nearly identical to Millbrook's. If the same program is adopted there, reading scores will improve by about 12 percent within two years.
questionStem: The adviser's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The factors that made the tutoring program effective in Millbrook are still present in the neighboring district today.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other reading-improvement initiative in the neighboring district could produce gains larger than 12 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Student reading scores in the neighboring district are currently lower than Millbrook's were five years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every student in the neighboring district would participate in the tutoring program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tutoring program's costs are comparable to those of existing programs in the neighboring district.

explanations.correct: The argument predicts the same outcome from the same program. If the background conditions that made the program work in Millbrook (funded libraries, trained tutors, cooperating parents) are absent in the neighboring district today, the prediction fails. Demographics alone don't guarantee those conditions. Negate A and the conclusion no longer follows.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — the argument predicts this program's effect, not a comparison to other initiatives.
explanations.C: Out of scope — current baseline is not a link in the inference from program to improvement.
explanations.D: Too strong — universal participation is not part of the Millbrook precedent or the prediction.
explanations.E: Out of scope — cost comparisons are not a link in the argument.

difficultyReason: Ethics argument has a conditional-style gap: the conclusion that the executive acted wrongly depends on a linking principle between duties to shareholders and the specific disclosure at issue. Multiple distractors shift scope.
stimulus: Ethicist: Corporate executives have a duty to disclose to shareholders any information that would materially affect the value of their shares. When CEO Lanier learned of the impending product recall, she waited two weeks before informing shareholders. Therefore, Lanier violated her duty to the shareholders.
questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any information about a product recall would materially affect the value of a company's shares.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CEOs who delay disclosing material information always do so for personal financial gain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lanier had a duty to disclose the recall before she was legally required to do so.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shareholders would have sold their shares had they been informed of the recall sooner.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two weeks is the longest an executive can reasonably delay any corporate disclosure.

explanations.correct: The premise is about materially-share-affecting information; the conclusion is about this recall. Without the bridge that the recall qualifies as such information, the duty the ethicist cited doesn't attach. Negate A — not all recall information materially affects share value — and Lanier's particular recall may fall outside the duty, so the conclusion does not follow.
explanations.B: Too strong — motive is not required for a duty violation.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the argument is about ethical duty, not legal timing.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — shareholder reaction is not what 'material' means in the stated duty.
explanations.E: Too strong — a general timing rule is not needed; the ethicist only needs this delay to have violated the duty.
